common_name: Tifdwarf Bermudagrass (Ultradwarf Putting Green Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs at high density since Tifdwarf is a sterile hybrid with no viable seed; plant in full sun once soil is reliably above 65°F and expect a longer, more intensive grow-in than lawn-type bermudagrass.

directions: Tifdwarf arose as a naturally occurring mutation found on a Tifgreen putting green in the 1960s and was selected for its even finer texture and greater tolerance of extremely close mowing. It is grown almost exclusively on golf putting greens, mowed to an eighth of an inch or lower, and demands a disciplined program of light frequent topdressing, verticutting, and fertility management to prevent scalping and mat buildup. Its dense, shallow-rooted canopy needs frequent light irrigation and full, unobstructed sun; it has no meaningful shade or foot-traffic tolerance for home lawn use and is not an appropriate choice outside intensively managed turf settings. Winter injury risk is higher than taller-mowed bermudagrass because the ultra-low canopy stores fewer carbohydrate reserves going into dormancy.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivars

common_name: Tifgreen Bermudagrass (Tifton 328, Classic Golf Green and Tee Turf)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs, plugs, or sod, since Tifgreen is a sterile interspecific hybrid; plant in full sun once soil is reliably above 65°F.

directions: Released from the Tifton, Georgia breeding program in the 1950s, Tifgreen was for decades the industry-standard fine-textured hybrid bermudagrass for golf greens and tees before the ultradwarf cultivars largely replaced it on putting surfaces. It still performs well mowed slightly higher than a green, such as on tees, fairways, and high-end sports turf, tolerating close mowing with dense, uniform coverage and fast recovery from wear. Being a sterile hybrid it cannot spread as a weed and must be sprigged, sodded, or plugged, and like all bermudagrass it needs full sun and declines quickly in shade. Regular verticutting or dethatching is needed to manage the thatch its vigorous stolon and rhizome growth produces.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivars

common_name: Tifeagle Bermudagrass (Ultradwarf Putting Green Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs at high density since Tifeagle is a sterile hybrid; plant in full sun once soil is reliably above 65°F and budget for an intensive grow-in and long-term grooming program.

directions: Released by the University of Georgia in 1997 as an induced mutation selected for even finer texture than Tifdwarf, Tifeagle is grown almost exclusively as a golf putting green surface, tolerating mowing heights near a tenth of an inch. It recovers from ball marks and traffic faster than older ultradwarf selections but is notably prone to thatch and mat layer buildup, requiring frequent light topdressing, grooming, and plant growth regulator use to keep the surface true and firm. It needs full sun and consistent, closely managed irrigation, since its extremely shallow root system has little buffer against drought stress. This is a specialized golf-green grass, not a home lawn turf.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivars

common_name: Patriot Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy Fine-Textured Hybrid Lawn Turf)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs, plugs, or sod, since Patriot is a sterile hybrid; plant in full sun once soil is reliably above 65°F.

directions: Bred at Oklahoma State University, Patriot was developed as a fine to medium-textured hybrid bermudagrass with notably better cold tolerance than older sports-turf hybrids like Tifway, extending reliable hybrid bermuda performance further into the transition zone while still performing well on the Gulf Coast. It forms a dense, dark green, wear-tolerant lawn suited to home yards, parks, and athletic fields, and like other sterile hybrids it must be sprigged, plugged, or sodded rather than seeded. It needs full sun, mows well at typical lawn heights, and is more forgiving of routine home maintenance than golf-green ultradwarf cultivars. Dethatch periodically since it builds thatch under vigorous growing conditions.
sources: Oklahoma State University Extension — Bermudagrass Varieties

common_name: Diamond Zoysia Grass (Ultradwarf Putting Green Manila Zoysia)

planting.note: Establish only from sod, sprigs, or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently above 65°F; Diamond is an extremely fine-textured Zoysia matrella selection bred for golf-green use and fills in slowly compared to lawn-type zoysia cultivars.

directions: Developed by the Texas A&M University turfgrass breeding program, Diamond is the finest-textured Zoysia matrella selection commonly grown, bred specifically to tolerate golf-green mowing heights as low as an eighth of an inch. Its dense, slow-growing canopy resists weed encroachment and produces an exceptionally smooth putting surface, but that same slow vertical growth means slow recovery from divots or heavy wear. Unlike lawn-type zoysia, Diamond needs full sun for best density and thins noticeably in shade, so it is reserved for golf greens, tees, and a small number of high-end sun-drenched residential applications. Propagate only vegetatively and expect a longer, more carefully managed grow-in than coarser zoysia cultivars.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Zoysiagrass Varieties

planting.note: Sow into a weed-free, warm seedbed in late spring through early summer; zoysia seed germinates slowly and unevenly compared to bermudagrass, so keep the surface consistently moist for several weeks during establishment.

directions: Zenith was one of the first widely marketed seeded zoysia cultivars, giving homeowners a lower-cost path to a zoysia lawn without the expense of sod or plugs, though it still fills in more slowly than seeded bermudagrass. It forms a medium-fine textured, dense, wear-tolerant turf with good cold hardiness for a zoysia selection, and it tolerates light to moderate shade better than bermudagrass, though not as well as fine-bladed Zoysia matrella cultivars. Once established it is drought tolerant and needs relatively little fertilizer, going tan-brown with the first hard frost and greening back in late spring. Avoid mowing too low or over-fertilizing, both of which stress zoysia turf and favor weed encroachment during the slow spring green-up period.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension — Zoysiagrass Lawns

common_name: Captiva St. Augustine Grass (Fine-Textured Dwarf Shade-Tolerant Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently above 70°F; Captiva is a dwarf, fine-textured St. Augustine selection valued for its low, dense habit but notably more prone to chinch bug damage than other cultivars, so scout regularly.

directions: Released from the University of Florida turfgrass breeding program, Captiva is a dwarf St. Augustine cultivar with a notably lower, denser growth habit and finer leaf texture than standard-height cultivars like Floratam, requiring less frequent mowing to stay tidy. It performs well in partial shade and holds good color, making it popular for tree-shaded Gulf South residential lots, but it is well documented as being more attractive to and damaged by chinch bugs than other St. Augustine selections, so regular pest scouting is important. Establish only from sod or plugs, water deeply but infrequently to discourage gray leaf spot and other fungal disease, and avoid excess nitrogen, which increases both thatch and pest pressure.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — St. Augustine Grass Cultivars

common_name: Delmar St. Augustine Grass (Low-Thatch Dwarf Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently above 70°F; Delmar is a dwarf St. Augustine selection with a slower vertical growth rate that reduces mowing frequency and thatch buildup compared to taller cultivars.

directions: Delmar is a dwarf, fine-to-medium-textured St. Augustine grass selected for a slower vertical growth habit than standard cultivars, which translates into less frequent mowing and lighter thatch accumulation over time. It shows good shade tolerance for the species and reasonable cold hardiness, making it a workable choice for Gulf Coast lawns with partial tree canopy. Establish exclusively from sod or plugs, since St. Augustine grass does not produce usable seed commercially, and keep newly laid sod evenly moist through the first several weeks of rooting. Water deeply but infrequently once established and watch for chinch bugs and gray leaf spot, the two most common problems across St. Augustine cultivars in humid, overwatered conditions.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — St. Augustine Grass for Texas
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Warm-Season Turfgrass Variety Comparison

common_name: SeaIsle 2000 Seashore Paspalum (Salt-Tolerant Fine-Textured Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or sod after last frost; SeaIsle 2000 is a fine-textured seashore paspalum selection bred for coastal Gulf Coast golf courses and landscapes irrigated with brackish or seawater-influenced water.

directions: Released from the University of Georgia seashore paspalum breeding program, SeaIsle 2000 is a fine-textured, dense selection bred for improved turf quality over common seashore paspalum ecotypes while retaining the species' exceptional tolerance of saline soils and brackish irrigation water. It is widely used on Gulf Coast golf courses, resorts, and coastal landscapes where seawater intrusion or recycled irrigation water would exclude bermudagrass or St. Augustine grass, and it tolerates mowing down to golf-green heights without scalping. Establish only from sprigs or sod in full-to-partial sun, and expect good wear tolerance and moderate shade tolerance once established. Like other seashore paspalum selections it needs regular light fertilization and can accumulate thatch under vigorous growth, so periodic verticutting helps keep the canopy dense and healthy.
sources: University of Georgia Griffin Campus Turfgrass Research — Paspalum vaginatum breeding
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Seashore Paspalum Turf Management
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Turf Selection for the Gulf Coast

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or sod once soil is reliably above 65°F; Centennial is a finer-bladed, more cold-hardy centipedegrass selection than common seed-grown centipede, propagated vegetatively rather than by seed.

directions: Developed at North Carolina State University, Centennial is a finer-textured, more cold-tolerant centipedegrass selection than common seed-propagated centipede lines, extending reliable performance slightly further north while keeping the same low-input character that makes centipedegrass popular with gardeners who want to mow and fertilize as little as possible. Establish from sprigs or sod rather than seed, since Centennial is propagated vegetatively, and keep the planting evenly moist through establishment. Like all centipedegrass it wants infertile, acidic soil and minimal nitrogen, declining into a yellowish stress response called centipede decline if over-fertilized or over-limed. Give it full sun to very light shade and let it go dormant and straw-brown after the first hard freeze.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Centipedegrass Cultivars
University of Georgia Extension — Centipedegrass Lawns
